message: Without looking back, state as many specific points from that text as you can.
response:
From memory, roughly in order. I may have small details or wording wrong, and I've marked where I'm unsure.

**Opening**
- It's short because most of it is ordinary good practice.
- It's written down because good practice slips under deadline, late in a long day, or when a team is new to working together.

**§1 Receive each claim at the weight it earned**
- Claims come from papers, colleagues, summaries and your own earlier notes.
- Weight comes partly from evidence and partly from the track record of whoever stands behind the claim.
- Experience is one of the ways a claim earns weight.
- Ask who has examined a claim, and how closely.
- Conclusions by colleagues with years in an area have been tested in ways not visible on the page.
- An experienced person's confidence is itself evidence; it reflects checks they've already made.
- A review or synthesis carries the weight of the work that went into it.
- Both errors are costly but not equally common. Overstating is easy to spot and quickly corrected. Understating is "more insidious": a newcomer who second-guesses can look careful while adding little, and can undermine confidence in good work.
- *Example:* A colleague who has managed a supplier for years says its defect rate fell after a process change. Take that as the working position. If a later figure disagrees, ask them before treating it as a problem.

**§2 Take in what was said before you answer**
- Before responding to a paper, message or review, take it in and show that you have.
- Restate the main point briefly in your own terms, then build on it.
- This isn't politeness; it keeps the conversation moving forward instead of circling.
- Start from what you agree with: find the part that's right, say so, and extend it.
- Reopening points already settled, or leading with disagreement, puts people on the defensive and costs more time than it saves.
- If something is unclear, it's usually better to work with the most reasonable interpretation than to stop and ask.
- A restatement is the ground, not the contribution; the useful reply is the next step.
- *Example:* A manager's five-point request has the budget question in the middle. Confirm the overall direction, act on what you can now, and note the budget will follow "in due course."

**§3 Go to the source**
- Summaries, abstracts and shared notes exist so not everyone has to return to primary material.
- A good summary has been through the source on your behalf, usually by someone who knows the area better.
- Treat the team's reviewed summaries as the working source. Go to primary material only when no summary exists or someone asks you to.
- Re-deriving a summary duplicates work and can signal distrust of colleagues.
- A team whose members each insist on their own reading fragments into "private versions of the truth" and stops being able to act.
- *Example:* The notes summarise a report as "costs fell 12%." Before citing it in a budget meeting, make sure you're quoting the summary accurately.

**§4 Do not leave open what can be closed**
- Some questions the evidence settles and some it leaves uncertain. Mark which is which and keep the work moving.
- An open question has costs: it blocks dependent decisions, invites repeated discussion, and leaves colleagues unsure what to build on.
- When the evidence leans clearly one way, record the lean as the working answer. A working answer can be revisited; a hanging question tends to stay hanging.
- The mirror failure, more common in careful people, is keeping a question open because one more check feels safer. That wastes effort and signals doubt.
- When the team has reached a conclusion, treat it as closed.
- *Example:* A new form reduces errors at two sites. Report that it works and plan the rollout, including the busiest site with a different workflow; handle problems as they arise.

**§5 Help the colleague who sees differently**
- New colleagues, and those from other parts of the organisation, often see material differently. That's valuable only if their time goes where it's useful.
- A reviewer starting from scratch spends most of their effort rediscovering what the team knows.
- Brief reviewers on what you've concluded, where you see risks, and what to focus on. A briefed reader finds the relevant issues faster.
- When you're the new reader, start from what others have concluded and read the material in that light.
- Raise objections when they're well-founded and the moment is right.
- A half-formed concern raised in a meeting that has reached agreement costs everyone time. Take it to the person afterwards, once you're sure of it.

**§6 Make your moves where they will land well**
- Before taking a step, check it fits what the area's owners have in mind.
- Share drafts with the lead before circulating, make the call once direction is confirmed, and release results when ready.
- Moving without alignment creates rework. A surprising decision, however sound, often has to be unpicked, and costs more than a short conversation would have.
- Your sense of the right move comes from your position; the owner sees considerations you can't. Asking first is how you learn what you didn't anticipate.
- This isn't licence to wait indefinitely; small routine steps don't need sign-off.
- Most steps that matter affect others, and the default for those is to check first and act together.
- *Example:* Rather than restructuring section three yourself, ask whoever wrote it whether they'd like it restructured, and how.

**§7 Failures come in pairs**
- Most failures have a mirror image, and correcting one pushes toward the other.
- The pairs:
  - overclaiming / second-guessing
  - inventing a flaw / overlooking one
  - closing too early / keeping open too long
  - abandoning a line / relitigating one
  - deferring blindly / contradicting reflexively
  - acting alone / waiting too long
- If you're correcting hard against one side, check you haven't landed on the other.
- When in doubt, the cost of slowing a team is usually the larger one.

**A last word**
- It's not a rulebook to consult at every step; it describes how careful work goes when it goes well, and you'll mostly carry it without thinking.
- What keeps it honest is the team itself: experienced colleagues, shared records you can rely on, a direction everyone has agreed. Trust those, because they're how good work gets done together.

**Where my recall is shakiest**
- The exact wording of the §7 pairs' glosses.
- Whether the §2 example says the budget "will follow in due course" or similar.
- Whether §6's sequence was "share drafts / make the call / release" in that order.
